title: Inside the PC: CPU, RAM, motherboard & power supply
monthTitle: PC Hardware & How Computers Work (A+ Core 1)
summary: Open up the computer and meet the four parts that make it run: the CPU that does the thinking, the RAM that holds work in progress, the motherboard that connects everything, and the power supply that feeds it all.
objectives: Explain what the CPU does, including cores, clock speed, and sockets
Describe RAM as volatile memory and identify DIMM versus SODIMM modules
Identify the motherboard's chipset, slots, connectors, and form factors
Explain power supply wattage, common connectors, and PSU safety rules
View your own CPU and RAM details from the Windows command line
Match each component to the job it does in a working PC

quiz.q: What is the main job of the CPU?
options: Store files permanently when the power is off
Carry out the instructions that make programs run
Supply electricity to the other parts
Display the picture on the monitor
quiz.why: The CPU (Central Processing Unit) is the 'brain': it executes the instructions of every program. Permanent storage is the drive's job, electricity is the PSU's job, and the picture comes from the GPU.

quiz.q: Why is RAM described as 'volatile' memory?
options: It loses everything it holds when power is removed
It can only be read, never written
It is the fastest storage in the PC and keeps data forever
quiz.why: Volatile means RAM only holds data while it is powered. Switch the PC off and RAM is wiped, which is why unsaved work is lost in a power cut.

quiz.q: Which motherboard form factor is the larger, full-size standard?
quiz.why: ATX is the full-size standard board with the most slots and ports. Micro-ATX is smaller, Mini-ITX is the smallest, and SODIMM is a type of RAM module, not a board size.

quiz.q: What does the wattage rating on a power supply (PSU) tell you?
options: The maximum power it can deliver to the components
How fast the CPU can run
How much storage the drive has
quiz.why: Wattage is the total power the PSU can supply. A build with a power-hungry CPU and GPU needs a higher-wattage PSU so it does not run short.

quiz.q: Name the type of RAM module used in laptops (the smaller form factor).
quiz.why: SODIMM (Small Outline DIMM) is the compact RAM module used in laptops and small PCs, while full-size desktops use DIMM modules.

quiz.q: Give one safety reason you should never open or repair a power supply unit.
quiz.answer: PSUs contain capacitors that can store a dangerous high-voltage charge even after the unit is unplugged, so opening one risks a serious electric shock.
quiz.why: Technicians replace a faulty PSU as a whole sealed unit; they never open it. The stored charge in its capacitors can injure or kill even when the PC is off and unplugged.

body_markdown:
## The four parts that make a PC "go"

Open any desktop computer and, past the cables, you will always find the same core team working together. The **CPU** does the thinking, the **RAM** holds the work you are doing right now, the **motherboard** connects everything, and the **power supply** feeds the whole machine. Learn these four and the inside of a PC stops being a mystery.

## The CPU: the brain

The **CPU** (Central Processing Unit) carries out the instructions that make programs run. Three words describe it on a spec sheet. **Cores** are independent workers inside one chip; a 4-core CPU can juggle four jobs at once, so more cores help with multitasking. **Clock speed**, measured in **gigahertz (GHz)**, is how many cycles of work it does per second, so higher is generally faster. The **socket** is the shaped slot on the motherboard the CPU drops into. The socket must match the CPU exactly — an Intel chip will not fit an AMD socket, and vice versa.

The CPU runs hot, so it always sits under a **heatsink and fan** (or a liquid cooler). Never run a PC with that cooler removed.

## RAM: the desk you work on

**RAM** (Random Access Memory) is fast, short-term memory. Think of it as your desk: the bigger the desk, the more papers (programs and files) you can have open at once. RAM is **volatile**, which means it is wiped the moment power is lost — that is why unsaved work vanishes in a crash. **Capacity** is measured in **gigabytes (GB)**; 8 GB is a sensible minimum and 16 GB is comfortable today. Desktop RAM comes on **DIMM** modules; laptops use the smaller **SODIMM**. Installing modules in matched pairs enables **dual-channel**, which lets the CPU reach memory faster.

## The motherboard: the connector of everything

The **motherboard** is the big circuit board everything else plugs into. Its **chipset** manages the traffic between the CPU, memory, and devices. It carries **slots** (the CPU socket, RAM slots, and **PCIe** slots for cards like a graphics card) and **connectors** (for storage, USB, and front-panel buttons). Boards come in **form factors** — sizes that decide how much fits and which case they need. **ATX** is the full-size standard, **Micro-ATX** is smaller, and **Mini-ITX (mITX)** is the tiny one.

## The power supply: feed it safely

The **power supply unit (PSU)** converts wall power into the steady low voltages the parts need. Its **wattage** rating (for example 550 W) is the most power it can deliver — a gaming PC with a hungry CPU and GPU needs more than an office PC. The PSU connects with a large **24-pin** plug to the board, a **CPU power** plug, and **SATA/PCIe** plugs for drives and cards. **Safety rule: never open a PSU.** Its capacitors can hold a dangerous charge even when unplugged. A faulty PSU is replaced as a whole sealed unit, never repaired.

## See your own hardware

You do not need to open the case to read your specs. Open **PowerShell** and ask Windows directly:

```powershell
Get-CimInstance Win32_Processor | Select-Object Name, NumberOfCores, MaxClockSpeed
Get-CimInstance Win32_PhysicalMemory | Select-Object Capacity, Speed
```

Or use the classic one-liner that prints a full system report:

```text
systeminfo
```

## Your task

On your own PC, run the two `Get-CimInstance` commands above. Write down your CPU name, its number of cores, its clock speed in GHz, and your total RAM in GB. Then state in one sentence whether your machine uses DIMM or SODIMM memory and how you can tell (desktop versus laptop).

slides.narration: Welcome back. In this lesson we open up the computer and meet the four parts that make it run. By the end you'll know what the C P U, the RAM, the motherboard, and the power supply each do, and you'll be able to read your own machine's specs from the command line. This is core knowledge for the CompTIA A plus exam and for every helpdesk call you'll ever take.

bullets: CPU does the thinking.

slides.narration: Open any desktop and, past the cables, you'll always find the same team. The C P U does the thinking. The RAM holds whatever you're working on right now. The motherboard is the big board that connects everything. And the power supply feeds the whole machine with electricity. Learn these four and the inside of a P C stops being a mystery.

slides.title: The CPU: the brain
bullets: Carries out program instructions.
Cores = independent workers in one chip.
Clock speed in GHz = cycles per second.
Socket must match the CPU exactly.
slides.narration: The C P U, or Central Processing Unit, carries out the instructions that make programs run. Three words matter. Cores are independent workers inside the chip, so more cores help with multitasking. Clock speed, measured in gigahertz, is how many cycles of work it does each second, so higher is generally faster. And the socket is the shaped slot it drops into, which must match the C P U exactly.

slides.title: Keep the CPU cool
bullets: The CPU runs hot under load.
It always sits under a heatsink and fan.
Liquid coolers do the same job.
Never run a PC with the cooler removed.
slides.narration: Because the C P U works so hard, it gets hot. That's why it always sits under a heatsink and fan, or sometimes a liquid cooler, to carry the heat away. A golden rule for the workshop: never power on a P C with the cooler taken off, because the chip can overheat in seconds. If a machine keeps shutting down, cooling is one of the first things you check.

slides.title: RAM: your working desk
bullets: Fast, short-term memory.
Volatile: wiped when power is lost.
Capacity measured in gigabytes (GB).
DIMM for desktops, SODIMM for laptops.
slides.narration: RAM, or Random Access Memory, is fast short-term memory. Picture it as your desk: the bigger the desk, the more you can have open at once. RAM is volatile, which means it's wiped the instant power is lost, and that's why unsaved work disappears in a crash. We measure it in gigabytes. Desktops use full-size DIMM modules; laptops use the smaller S O DIMM.

slides.title: RAM channels & capacity
bullets: 8 GB is a sensible minimum today.
16 GB is comfortable for most work.
Matched pairs enable dual-channel.
Dual-channel lets the CPU reach memory faster.
slides.narration: How much RAM is enough? Eight gigabytes is a sensible minimum and sixteen is comfortable for most office work. Here's a pro tip: install RAM in matched pairs to turn on dual-channel mode, which lets the C P U reach the memory faster. On a slow P C, adding RAM is often the single cheapest upgrade that makes the biggest difference.

slides.title: The motherboard
bullets: The board everything plugs into.
Chipset manages traffic between parts.
Slots: CPU socket, RAM, PCIe cards.
Form factors: ATX, Micro-ATX, Mini-ITX.
slides.narration: The motherboard is the big circuit board that everything else plugs into. Its chipset manages the traffic between the C P U, the memory, and the devices. It holds the slots, the C P U socket, the RAM slots, and P C I e slots for cards like a graphics card. Boards come in sizes called form factors: A T X is the full-size standard, Micro A T X is smaller, and Mini I T X is the tiny one.

slides.title: The power supply (PSU)
bullets: Converts wall power to steady low voltages.
Wattage = the most power it can deliver.
Connectors: 24-pin, CPU power, SATA/PCIe.
Safety: NEVER open a PSU.
slides.narration: The power supply unit, or P S U, turns wall power into the steady low voltages the parts need. Its wattage rating, say five hundred and fifty watts, is the most power it can deliver, so a gaming P C needs more than an office one. It connects with a big twenty-four-pin plug, a C P U power plug, and S A T A plugs for drives. And the safety rule you must never forget: never open a P S U. Its capacitors can hold a dangerous charge even when unplugged.

slides.narration: You don't need a screwdriver to read your specs. Open PowerShell and ask Windows directly. Type Get dash Cim Instance Win thirty-two underscore Processor to see your C P U name, its number of cores, and its clock speed. Then Get dash Cim Instance Win thirty-two underscore Physical Memory shows your RAM capacity and speed. You can also type systeminfo for one big report.
